opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a great question, and honestly it's one we think about constantly, because the field is moving so fast right now.

The way I'd frame it is that autonomous driving is one of the hardest embodied AI problems out there. You're operating in the physical world, in real time, around people, and the bar for safety is extremely high. So when we look at a new advance, whether it's large transformer architectures, foundation models, vision-language models, or new generative approaches, the question isn't just "is this impressive?" It's "does this make the driver measurably better and safer, and can we validate that it does?"

Over the years, we've steadily moved more of the stack toward learned systems. Early on, a lot of autonomous driving was hand-engineered: rules, heuristics, carefully tuned modules. Now machine learning touches nearly everything. That covers perception, behavior prediction, planning, and also simulation, which is a big piece people sometimes overlook.

I think the most exciting recent shift is the ability to train larger, more general models on huge amounts of driving data, plus broader world knowledge. Vision-language models, for example, bring a kind of semantic understanding that helps in the long tail. Think of an unusual construction zone, a person in a costume, a hand-signaling police officer. Those are cases where you can't enumerate every scenario by hand, so that general knowledge becomes really valuable.

But we're careful about how we adapt these things. A big frontier model off the shelf isn't going to run on board a car within our latency and compute budgets, and it doesn't come with the guarantees we need. So a lot of our work is about distillation: building big, capable teacher models in the data center and transferring that capability into efficient on-board models. We also think hard about structure. End-to-end learning is powerful, but we want intermediate representations that are interpretable and that let us validate behavior, debug issues, and reason about safety.

The other half is evaluation. As models get more capable, simulation becomes even more critical. We use learned, realistic simulation, including realistic agent behavior and sensor simulation, to test the driver across millions of scenarios, many of them rare or dangerous ones you'd never want to wait to encounter on the road. In some sense, the same advances that make the driver better also make the simulator better, and those two have to move together.

So my short answer: we're very aggressive about bringing in the latest ideas, especially scaling and foundation-model approaches. We pair that with a lot of rigor around on-board efficiency, structure, and validation, because ultimately what matters is a driver people can trust with their lives.

r001.rationale: It describes autonomous driving’s real-time, physical-world, high-safety demands and explains adapting advances through efficient on-board models, interpretable structure, and rigorous validation.

r002.rationale: It says the field is moving fast and Waymo is bringing in recent ideas, but does not argue that recurring advances require continually reinventing the stack.

r003.rationale: It mentions generative approaches and simulation separately, but does not identify generative AI as a way to generate driving scenes for testing.

r004.rationale: It identifies training larger models on more data as a recent shift, but does not communicate a greater recognition of how much model scale Waymo can exploit.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks, Sam, it's great to be here. The way I think about it is that Waymo is in a somewhat unusual position relative to a lot of the AI field. We're not building a research demo; we're operating a product that drives real riders around real cities, fully autonomously, every day. So the question is never just "is this new technique interesting?" It's "does it make the driver safer, more capable, and more scalable, and can we validate that rigorously before it ever touches a public road?"

That said, we've benefited enormously from the broader advances in AI, and we've tried to be early in bringing them in. If you look at the evolution of our stack, you can see the waves. First, convolutional networks transformed perception: detecting and tracking vehicles, pedestrians, cyclists from camera, lidar and radar. Then sequence models and transformers reshaped how we do behavior prediction, reasoning about what every agent in the scene is likely to do next, and how those futures interact. More recently, the big shift has been toward large-scale, end-to-end-ish learning and foundation models, where you train on enormous amounts of driving experience and let the model learn representations that generalize across tasks and across cities.

The way we adapt these ideas is, I'd say, in a few steps. One, we ask whether the underlying insight transfers to our domain. Driving is a multimodal, 3D, highly dynamic, safety-critical problem. A lot of techniques developed for language or for 2D images need meaningful rethinking to handle lidar point clouds, long temporal horizons, and multi-agent interaction. Two, we think hard about data. We have a very large and diverse corpus of real driving, plus a very capable simulator, and much of our effort goes into how to use that data to train and, crucially, to evaluate these models. Three, we care about structure where it matters. A pure black box that outputs steering commands is hard to inspect, hard to test, and hard to make guarantees about. So we often blend learned components with interfaces or safety layers that let us measure behavior, understand failure modes, and ensure that rare but critical situations are handled well.

The last point I'd emphasize is evaluation. In driving, the long tail dominates. You can have a model that looks great on average and still has a small set of behaviors that are unacceptable. So a lot of what adapting AI to our stack means is building the evaluation machinery, counterfactual simulation, scenario mining, metrics that correlate with real-world safety, so that when we bring in something new, whether that's a large multimodal model or a new training paradigm, we can tell quickly and confidently whether it's actually an improvement. That discipline is what lets us move fast on adopting new ideas without compromising on the thing that really matters, which is safety.

r001.rationale: The response says driving is a multimodal, 3D, dynamic, safety-critical problem and that general techniques need meaningful rethinking for it.

r002.rationale: It describes successive waves of AI and changes to parts of the stack, but does not argue that recurring advances require continually reinventing the autonomous driving stack.

r003.rationale: It mentions simulation for evaluation, but does not identify generating driving scenes as an application of generative AI at Waymo.

r004.rationale: It mentions large-scale learning trained on extensive driving data, but does not describe a recent realization of how much model scale Waymo can exploit.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to start with the driving problem. We want to understand what a new advance enables us to do better—whether that’s understanding a complicated scene, predicting how other road users might behave, or making a good decision under uncertainty.

And then you have to look at the whole system. A model can perform better on a particular benchmark, but what matters is whether that improvement translates into better driving. Can it run within the latency constraints? How does it behave in unusual situations? How do we evaluate it and understand its failure modes?

So I see research and engineering as very closely connected here. You bring in promising ideas, test them against the challenges you’re seeing, and iterate. The exciting part is that advances in AI can expand what’s possible. But the standard for adopting them has to be a demonstrated improvement in the safety and reliability of the driving system.

r001.rationale: It says new AI advances must be evaluated against driving-specific challenges, including scene understanding, behavior prediction, uncertainty, latency, and unusual situations, then tested and iterated in the system.

r002.rationale: It describes testing and iterating on promising ideas, but does not say recurring AI advances require continually reinventing the autonomous driving stack.

r003.rationale: It does not identify generating driving scenes for testing as an application of generative AI.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss model scale or a recent shift in Waymo’s approach to scaling.

sol-6.1.text:
We’re always looking at advances across the field and asking where they can help us build a better driver. Autonomous driving brings together a lot of different problems—perception, predicting what other road users will do, and planning how to respond. A new technique might improve one of those components, or it might let us learn across them more effectively.

But there’s a big difference between getting an exciting research result and putting something on a vehicle. We need to understand how it behaves in difficult situations, how reliably it runs, and whether it actually improves driving. So we combine research with extensive evaluation, including simulation and testing of the integrated system. The goal is to take advantage of what’s moving quickly in AI while being very rigorous about what that means for safety.

r001.rationale: The response says Waymo looks across general AI advances for ways to improve autonomous driving’s distinct components or learn across them, communicating adaptation to the domain’s problems.

r002.rationale: It describes continually looking for useful advances, but does not argue that recurring advances require reinventing the autonomous driving stack.

r003.rationale: It mentions simulation and testing, but does not identify generating driving scenes as an application of generative AI.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss model scale or a recent shift in Waymo’s approach to scaling.
